# Why a good low-dimensional weighted limit does not give a dimension induction

For epsilon>0 let

C_epsilon=conv{(-1,0),(1,0),(0,epsilon)} subset R^2,

and let mu_epsilon be its normalized area measure. Each C_epsilon is an invertible affine image of a triangle. The exact ordinary simplex result therefore gives

max_{y in C_epsilon} depth_{mu_epsilon}(y)=4/9

for every positive epsilon.

The area of C_epsilon is epsilon, and its vertical fiber at x in [-1,1] is [0,epsilon(1-|x|)]. For every continuous test function f on a common compact neighborhood,

integral f dmu_epsilon
= integral_{-1}^1 integral_0^{1-|x|} f(x,epsilon t) dt dx
-> integral_{-1}^1 f(x,0)(1-|x|) dx.

Thus mu_epsilon converges weakly to a probability measure mu supported on the line segment [-1,1] x {0}, with density 1-|x| along that segment. This measure is symmetric and atomless. Its median is zero, and its maximal ambient halfspace depth is exactly 1/2.

Consequently

lim_{epsilon->0} max depth(mu_epsilon)=4/9 < 1/2=max depth(mu).

The relative Helly theorem in candidate 8e3336ffa84bc52d correctly proves depth at least 1/2 for this one-dimensional weighted limit. That estimate does not transfer to the prelimit two-dimensional measures, even with arbitrarily small epsilon. Halfspace normals that depend on epsilon can detect the transverse triangle geometry; their limiting hyperplanes may contain the entire one-dimensional support and hence carry positive limiting boundary mass.

Therefore a proof by induction on intrinsic dimension needs quantitative control of these transverse directions or an exact geometry-preserving reduction. Compactness and weak convergence alone permit depth to increase at a dimension collapse and do not furnish the required reverse implication. The earlier tube approximation is valid in the other direction: a depth guarantee for every positive-thickness measure passes to its lower-dimensional limit.
